comment: Chapter 5, Future proofing the Architecture, discusses AI, genomics, wearables and edge computing, but the document contains no mention of post-quantum cryptography or cryptographic agility anywhere in its 254 pages. NIST finalised its first post-quantum standards in August 2024 (FIPS 203, 204 and 205), and lifelong health records are a prime harvest-now-decrypt-later target: data exchanged today must remain confidential for the lifetime of the patient. The term is also used loosely in the field. Programmes that describe a key-rotation mechanism as post-quantum readiness are describing something materially different from migration to the standardised post-quantum algorithms, and joint WHO and ITU guidance is well placed to hold that distinction for countries evaluating vendor claims.

public.suggestedRevision: Add cryptographic agility as a design requirement for trust and exchange infrastructure: every participant must be able to migrate keys and algorithms without changing identifiers, breaking existing trust relationships, or coordinating a simultaneous global migration. Identifiers that commit to key digests rather than to a named algorithm allow the signing algorithm to change without re-establishing identity, which is what makes an unsynchronised national migration feasible at all. Ask countries to distinguish that architectural property from algorithm migration itself, and to require both.
